titre: The Terrors of the Year 1000: A 19th-Century Myth
accroche: In 1833, Michelet writes that the medieval world believed in the end of the world with the year 1000. Historians see no general panic.
contenu_vulgarise:
In his *Histoire de France* (History of France), published in 1833, Jules Michelet describes a Middle Ages convinced that time was running out: “It was a universal belief in the Middle Ages that the world was to end with the year 1000 of the Incarnation.” According to him, faced with famines, everyone “wished to be out of their misery, at any price,” rather than wait; and the lords gave to the churches “for the remedy of [their] souls.” This scene has crossed generations of textbooks: at the turn of the year 1000, all of Christendom is supposed to have watched for the end of the world.

## A Story Built After the Fact

The problem is that this general panic is not found in the sources of the period. The Burgundian monk Raoul Glaber (985–1047), whose chronicle, the *Historiarum libri quinque*, covers the years 900 to 1044, did not begin writing it until around 1026, that is, more than twenty years after the year 1000. He writes in the past tense, years after the events, and the millennium that may have marked minds is that of the Passion, in 1033, not that of the Nativity.

According to Wikipedia's overview of these “terrors,” the story took shape in the Renaissance: Cardinal Baronius wrote in 1602 that the end of the world had supposedly been feared, relying on Glaber. It was then supposedly used during the Revolution to discredit the clergy, suspected of having stoked fear in order to obtain donations. Michelet, who takes up the motif of donations and of fear of the end, gives it its most famous literary form.

There is something even more awkward: the year 1000 was not a date that everyone could count. Only a small number of clerics, for the needs of the liturgy, knew how to calculate the year; the Christian era itself was not generalized until the second half of the 11th century, and the population oriented itself mostly by the seasons and religious feasts. So there was not, across the continent, a single evening to dread together.

In 1967, the historian Georges Duby reopened the case in *L'An Mil* (The Year 1000) and concluded that no collective panic had taken place, at most a diffuse unease among some. Even this thesis has since been contested, notably by Gouguenheim and Barthélemy, who judge that a Church preaching the imminent end would have lost its legitimacy. In a book of interviews published in 1995, *An 1000 – An 2000* (Year 1000, Year 2000), Duby returns to collective fears and to what they owe to the gap between the event and its telling.

## What This Changes

The point is not to mock Michelet, who wanted to bring the Middle Ages to life rather than to make them scholarly. It is to see how a story forged centuries after the events, repeated from book to book according to the use each author made of it, ends up passing for an established fact that no one goes back to check. A round number may have caused worry without there being evidence of it at the time; it was enough for evidence to be lent to it after the fact.

citation.texte: It was a universal belief in the Middle Ages that the world was to end with the year 1000 of the Incarnation.
citation.source: Histoire de France (History of France), Middle Ages, Book IV, chapter 1 (Flammarion ed., 1893)

carte.punch: Europe did not tremble in the year 1000. That happened later, in the history books.
carte.idee: The story of a Christendom in a panic as the year 1000 approached was built after the fact, from the chronicle of Raoul Glaber, written years after the events. Duby (1967) sees no general panic, and even his “diffuse unease” is contested.

quiz.question: Why does the story of a general panic as the year 1000 approached pose a problem for historians?
choix: Because the most-cited source was written only twenty-six years after the events
Because the year 1000 never existed in the Julian calendar
Because Raoul Glaber himself denied having written about this period
Because the Church destroyed all the documents relating to that year
quiz.explication: The main source invoked, Raoul Glaber, did not begin his chronicle until around 1026, years after the year 1000; the year 1000 was moreover not a date that everyone could count, since only a few clerics knew how to calculate the year. The year 1000 does exist in the calendar, Glaber never denied his chronicle, and nothing indicates a destruction of documents by the Church.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the historian Georges Duby conclude in 1967, in L'An Mil, about a collective panic in the year 1000?
choix: That a general panic did take place, but only in northern France
That no collective panic took place, at most a diffuse unease among some
That the panic was deliberately organized by the clergy to obtain donations
That sources are entirely lacking to rule on the question
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Duby concludes in 1967 that no collective panic took place, at most a diffuse unease among some, a thesis itself contested since; he does not limit this to northern France, does not accuse the clergy of organizing it, and does not say that sources are entirely lacking.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does a collective fear dated precisely to the year 1000 pose an additional problem, according to the entry?
choix: Because only a few clerics knew how to calculate the year, which was not generalized before the 11th century
Because the Julian calendar had no year 1000
Because the peasants believed in no form of religion at that time
Because the Church had officially abolished the counting of years in 999
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Only a small number of clerics knew how to calculate the year for the needs of the liturgy, and the Christian era was not generalized until the second half of the 11th century: there was therefore not, across the continent, a single evening that everyone could have dreaded together.
